findings.title: Validator with DB write double-counts block hits
findings.body: BlockedEmail.should_block? increments match_count and saves the record every time it is called, and EmailValidator calls it from validate_each. UsersController#create calls user.valid? and then user.save, which runs validations a second time. A single signup attempt therefore increments match_count twice and updates last_match_at twice. Any other valid? check also pollutes statistics. Validation must be read-only; counting should be done once outside validation.

findings.title: Case-sensitive exact block lookup is bypassable
findings.body: BlockedEmail.should_block? does BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first with the raw submitted value, with no downcasing or stripping. Blocked entry bad@spam.com will not match BAD@SPAM.COM, Bad@spam.com, or ' bad@spam.com '. An attacker blocked under one spelling can register by changing case or adding whitespace. Lookup and storage must be normalized the same way User emails are normalized with Email.downcase/strip.

findings.title: Non-atomic match_count increment loses updates
findings.body: BlockedEmail.should_block? does record.match_count += 1 followed by record.save. Under concurrent signups with the same blocked email two processes read the same count, increment, and save, so one increment is lost and last_match_at can be clobbered. It also runs full validations and callbacks for a counter update. Use an atomic counter update such as increment_counter/update_counters instead of read-modify-write.

findings.title: Domain whitelist/blacklist regex not anchored allows bypass
findings.body: email_in_restriction_setting? builds Regexp.new("@(#{domains})", true) with no end anchor and only dots escaped. A whitelist of example.com therefore matches user@example.com.evil.com because the pattern matches the substring @example.com. The same flaw causes blacklist false positives/negatives and lets an attacker pass a whitelist with a subdomain-suffix address. Anchor the domain to end of string and properly escape/parse the setting.

findings.title: change_email bypasses blocked-email validation
findings.body: UsersController#change_email downcases the new address, checks only whether it is already taken, then creates an email_token and sends an authorization email. It never checks SiteSetting email_domains_whitelist/blacklist or BlockedEmail.should_block?. A blocked address rejected at signup can therefore be adopted via the email-change flow, defeating the new block.

findings.title: Wrong dependent key prevents rejected-email UI update
findings.body: emailValidation is declared .property('accountEmail', 'rejectedEmails.@each') but rejectedEmails is an array of strings updated with pushObject. In Ember, pushObject notifies '[]', not '@each', which only observes properties on array items. After the server rejects an email the computed property does not recompute, so the inline invalid message is not shown and submitDisabled is not updated until the user edits the email field. The dependent key should be rejectedEmails.[].
